paper.title: Adaptive Crowdsourcing Algorithms for the Bandit Survey Problem

unmapped: single source of i.i.d. samples from a categorical distribution over n options; goal is to identify the mode (most probable option) and stop
unique_optimal_arm here means the correct answer is the unique most probable option
the stopping rule uses the number of options n
settings.definition_quote: a single-crowd stopping rule: an online algorithm which in every round inputs an option $x\in\options$ and decides whether to stop. ... characterized by two quantities that are to be minimized: the expected stopping time and the error rate

unmapped: arms are k crowds, each a categorical response distribution over n options; all crowds share the same unique most probable option x*
each crowd has a known per-round cost c_i; objective is expected total cost until stopping, plus error rate of the output option
performance measured relative to benchmark cost of best fixed crowd (or best distribution over crowds) under the same single-crowd stopping rule R_0
settings.definition_quote: In each round $t$, the algorithm picks some crowd $i=i_t$ and receives an independent sample from the corresponding response distribution $\D_i$. Eventually the algorithm must stop and output its guess for $x^*$. Each crowd $i$ has a known per-round cost $c_i$.

settings.name_in_paper: bandit survey problem with uniform costs
unmapped: crowds with categorical response distributions over n options, uniform costs (total cost = stopping time)
T is the time horizon of the stopping rule (stops at t=T at the latest)
settings.definition_quote: An important special case is uniform costs: all $c_i$ are equal; then the total cost is simply the stopping time.

algorithms.name: AlgUnif (uniform discretization + UCB over distributions on crowds, virtual rewards)

symbols.eps_gap: gap of the crowd: difference between largest and second-largest probabilities of its response distribution

tuning: errorC = sqrt(log(n N^2/delta)), N = number of samples so far

source.label: thm:single-crowd
source.quote: Consider the stopping rule~\refeq{eq:stopping-rule} with $\errorC = \sqrt{\log (\tfrac{n}{\delta}\, \NSamples{i}{t}^2 )}$, for some $\delta>0$. The error rate of this stopping rule is at most $O(\delta)$, and the expected stopping time is at most $O\left( \gap_i^{-2}\, \log \tfrac{n}{\delta \gap_i} \right)$.

results.notes: Expected stopping time of mode-identification stopping rule; mapped to sample_complexity.

source.label: thm:single-crowd
source.quote: The error rate of this stopping rule is at most $O(\delta)$

results.notes: Error rate = probability that the majority option at stopping is not x*.

conditions: applies to any single-crowd stopping rule with worst-case error rate less than delta

source.label: thm:single-crowd-LB
source.quote: Let $R_0$ be any single-crowd stopping rule with worst-case error rate less than $\delta$. When applied to a crowd with gap $\gap>0$, the expected stopping time of $R_0$ is at least $\Omega(\gap^{-2} \log \tfrac{1}{\delta})$.

results.notes: Stated as following from classical coin-tossing results; no proof given.

symbols.cost_istar: expected total cost of always choosing approximate best crowd i* = argmin c_i/eps_i^2 with stopping rule R_0 (coefficient 1, not inside O)
symbols.Lambda_c: sum over i != i* of (c_i (f_{i*} - f_i))^{-2}, with virtual reward f_i = eps_i/sqrt(c_i)

conditions: R_0 is a symmetric single-crowd stopping rule
R_0 must stop after at most T rounds
tuning: C = sqrt(8 log t) in the UCB index

source.label: thm:UCB
source.quote: Let $i^* = \argmin_i c_i/\gap^2_i$ be the approximate best crowd. Let $R_0$ be a symmetric single-crowd stopping rule. Assume $R_0$ must stop after at most $T$ rounds. Define \AlgUCB by~\refeq{eq:UCB-index} with $C = \sqrt{8\log t}$, for each round $t$. Let $\Lambda_i = ( c_i (f_{i^*} - f_i))^{-2}$ and $\Lambda = \sum_{i\neq i^*} \Lambda_i$. Then $ \cost(\AlgUCB|R_0) \leq \cost(i^*|R_0) + O(\Lambda \log T).$

results.notes: Quantity is expected total cost of the crowd-selection algorithm with the composite stopping rule; only the additive term is in O(). Proof is a sketch.

symbols.ratio_mu: sum_i c_i mu_i / min_i c_i mu_i for the algorithm's fixed distribution mu over crowds (at least K)
symbols.rho: worst-case error rate of the single-crowd stopping rule R_0

conditions: eps-simple instances: two options, one crowd with gap eps>0, all others gap 0
R_0 symmetric with worst-case error rate rho
composite stopping rule does not use the total crowd
algorithm is non-adaptive (samples crowds i.i.d. from fixed mu)

source.label: thm:LB
source.quote: Let $R_0$ be a symmetric single-crowd stopping rule with worst-case error rate $\rho$. Assume that the composite stopping rule does not use the total crowd. Consider a non-adaptive crowd-selection algorithm $\A$ whose distribution over crowds is $\mu$. Then for each $\gap>0$, the competitive ratio over the $\gap$-simple problem instances is at least $ \frac{\sum_i c_i\,\mu_i}{\min_i c_i\,\mu_i}\; (1-2k\rho)$, where $k$ is the number of crowds.

results.notes: Lower bound on competitive ratio (cost / deterministic benchmark cost) of non-adaptive algorithms; minimized ratio_mu equals K (round-robin with mu_i ~ 1/c_i).

symbols.f_star: maximal induced gap over distributions over crowds

conditions: R_0 is the total-crowd stopping rule: stop if empirical gap of total crowd > errorC/sqrt(t) or t = T

source.label: thm:AlgUnif
source.quote: Consider the \problem with uniform costs. Let $R_0$ be the single-crowd stopping rule given by~\refeq{eq:stopping-rule-total}. There exists a crowd-selection algorithm $\A$ such that $ \cost(\A|R_0) \leq O\left( (f^*)^{-(k+2)}\; \sqrt{\log T} \right).$

results.notes: Expected total cost (= stopping time). Algorithm described as possibly inefficient; comparator is the randomized benchmark (best distribution over crowds), mapped to best_policy.

symbols.bench_det: absolute deterministic benchmark cost with error rate rho and horizon T (coefficient 1)
symbols.Lambda_b: sum over i != i* of (eps_{i*} - eps_i)^{-2}

source.label: thm:UCB-bi
source.quote: (a) Deterministic benchmark. There exists a \Algorithm $(\A,R_0)$ such that \cost(\A|R_0) \leq \bench(i^*,\rho,T) + O(\Lambda \log T), where \Lambda = \sum_{i\neq i^*} (\bias_{i^*}-\bias_i )^{-2}, \error(\A|R_0) \leq (k+1)\,\rho.

results.notes: Bi-criteria: cost guarantee paired with error rate <= (K+1) rho (recorded separately).

symbols.rho: target worst-case error rate of the benchmark

results.notes: Part (a); the same (K+1)rho error bound holds in part (b).

symbols.bench_rand: absolute randomized benchmark cost with error rate rho and horizon T

tuning: quality parameter tuned so worst-case error rate matches benchmark

source.label: thm:UCB-bi
source.quote: (b) Randomized benchmark. There exists a \Algorithm $(\A,R_0)$ such that \cost(\A|R_0) \leq O(\log T \log \tfrac{1}{\rho}) \;(\bench(\mu^*,\rho,T))^{1+k/2} \\ \error(\A|R_0) &\leq (k+1)\,\rho.

symbols.rho: worst-case error rate of the symmetric single-crowd stopping rule R_0

conditions: composite stopping rule based on R_0 does not use the total crowd

source.label: lm:error-rate-LB
source.quote: Let $R_0$ be a symmetric single-crowd stopping rule with worst-case error rate $\rho$. Let $\A$ be a non-committing crowd-selection algorithm, and let $R$ be the composite stopping rule based on $R_0$ which does not use the total crowd. If $\A$ is used in conjunction with $R$, the worst-case error rate is at least $\rho\,(1-2k\rho)$, where $k$ is the number of crowds.

results.notes: Lower bound on worst-case error rate.
